abstract: This paper argues that scholarship on digital platforms and democracy should move beyond narrow causal-effects research toward analyzing platform collective behavior as a form of democratic infrastructure. Written in the context of the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA), it reframes how researchers should conceptualize and study platforms' role in democratic life.
key_claims: Causal-effects approaches are insufficient for understanding platforms' democratic significance.
Platform collective behavior should be conceptualized as democratic infrastructure.
The DSA era creates new opportunities and imperatives for rethinking platform research paradigms.
methods: Conceptual and theoretical argumentation rather than empirical study, situated in the regulatory context of the EU Digital Services Act.
findings: Not applicable — the paper is framed as a conceptual intervention rather than an empirical investigation (based on abstract only).
contributions: Proposes an infrastructural reframing of platform collective behavior for democracy research.
Connects political communication scholarship to the DSA regulatory environment.
Offers a critique of the dominance of causal-effects designs in platform-democracy research.
framing: The paper positions itself within political communication and platform studies, engaging debates about how digital platforms affect democracy and how European regulation (the DSA) reshapes the research agenda. It draws on infrastructure studies to challenge prevailing causal-effects paradigms.
